newsitem.title: USA: NYC watchdog says hospital deal should be delayed.
newsitem.headline: NYC watchdog says hospital deal should be delayed.

text.p: The New York City comptroller on Thursday said that the Board of Health and Hospitals Corp would be "irresponsible" if it went ahead with its vote, set for November 8 vote, on subleasing a public Brooklyn hospital.
Alan Hevesi, the city comptroller, called for a new public review as questions remain outstanding, from what care will be provided for the poor to how the hospital's performance will be monitored.

The agreement calls for PHS NY, a subsidiary of PHS Inc, which runs health-care companies in Cleveland and Philadelphia, to sublet the Coney Island Hospital. When the deal closes, PHS NY will pay $42.1 million to the Health and Hospitals Corp to pay off most of $49 million of outstanding debt The rest of the debt will be retired as it matures.
And PHS NY has agreed to spend a minimum of $25 million on capital improvements over five years, a Health and Hospital Corp spokesman said, because it wants a succesful hospital.

New York City has estimated it would save up to $100 million immediately and $30 million a year. Hevesi called such claims "incredible," saying the city now pays $45 million a year to subsidize the 17 Health and Hospitals Corp.

Despite Hevesi's criticisms, the Health and Hospitals Corp Chairwoman, Maria Mitchell, predicted the board on Friday will approve the deal, adding she expects to use it as a model for the city's efforts to sell two more of its hospitals. "I expect it will pass overwhelmingly."

Three board members who sued the Health and Hospitals Corp, saying it should have used the city's procurement process, dropped a motion for a temporary restraining order. They instead agreed to review the contract 48 hours before it is signed.

Mitchell defended both the agreement and the way in which it was set, saying any pact reached through negotiation required give and take. Some of Hevesi's criticisms concerned items that were dropped from early drafts, like his office's right to audit and abandoning a plan to have PHS NY make payments in lieu of taxes of as much as $2.3 million a year.

"If you pick out one thing as he does, or pick out several individual items, it is irrelevant because you are talking about items in abstract, and not the whole context of a product." Saying the pact provides the city with indigent care and access to quality healthcare, she concluded "We have an enormously sucessful final product, which has been subjected to major public scrutiny."
Mitchell added once the board votes on the Coney Island pact, it will refocus its efforts on a Queens hospital.

Hevesi, considered a potential Democratic challenger in next year's mayoral races, did not mince words in attacking an agreement that would further Republican Mayor Rudolph Giuliani's efforts to privatize three city hospitals.
"It is irresponsible to turn over a public hospital to a for-profit company for 200 years without understanding the effect of the deal on care and costs."

Although the total value of the hospital's assets is around $78 million, Hevesi, in prepared remarks, said a 200-year lease for approximately $48 million means the city is effectively selling it for that sum.

Hevesi said the pact does not guarantee that poor patients will still be cared for, adding the city would not be able to stop PHS NY from slashing core services like cardiology, noting one report found more intensive care patients died at a Cleveland hospital after PHS took it over. He also asked how much the city would pay to care for police officers and firefighters injured while on duty, and prisoners.
The Health and Hospital's Corp counsel has said that the tax-exempt status of up to $17 million of bonds issued for the Brooklyn hospital could be protected.

Karen Shaw, a senior vice president on the mayor's staff, said she expected the city's counsel to reach the same conclusion, adding nothing would be done to undermine the bonds' tax-exempt status. She noted the issue will be resolved before the deal closes.

However, the comptroller recommended that the Health and Hospital Corp first get a ruling from the Internal Revenue Service. "If the IRS. ultimately rules against the city, it will be more costly for Health and Hospitals Corp to finance capital improvements at other hospitals in its system."
